OpenAGI Dot · Prototype notes

Build the feeling.
Then make it smaller.

The voice-button idea is feasible to prototype with development modules. The tiny product in the images is a design target that needs a custom board and measured fit.

Parts researched. Hardware and companion integration not built.

Start on the bench.

A Seeed XIAO nRF52840 Sense already combines Bluetooth LE, a microphone, an RGB LED, and a battery charger on an approximately 21 × 18 mm board. Add a momentary button and prove hold-to-talk over USB before connecting a battery.

The board diagonal is about 28 mm. A circular first enclosure might land around 30–35 mm across before allowing for its actual battery, wiring, ports, and mounts. That is an estimate, not a validated minimum. A smaller Dot requires a custom PCB, antenna layout, power design, and enclosure stack-up.

The onboard RGB LED can test status colors. A continuous light ring needs its own LED placement and diffuser; a bright annulus is not supplied by the development board.

Yes to a little screen. Room for a voice.

A small OLED and speaker can be tested with the same prototype before the enclosure is designed. The important measurements are the complete modules, connectors, and acoustic space, not just the visible screen.

The OLED in the render illustrates a display window and interface. It is not a drawing of that rectangular module’s fitted assembly. Smaller bare speakers and display panels exist, but selecting them moves the project toward custom electronics, acoustic design, and manufacturing work.

For v0, keep replies on a phone, Mac, or headphones. Add a speaker to the larger bench prototype once microphone capture and latency work. Speech clarity, microphone feedback, and peak battery current determine whether local replies are worth the extra size.

Prove it in three steps.

  1. Interaction first. Test the button, microphone, BLE audio, host transcription, and status colors over USB. Hold a button for a short phrase; release should stop capture and yield one result.
  2. Fit actual parts. Measure current and runtime with the selected battery. Build a roomy printed enclosure around the physical stack. Test microphone openings, USB access, pocket presses, and necklace or wrist mounts.
  3. Miniaturize what works. Replace development boards with a custom PCB. Validate the antenna near the body, charging, battery protection, diffuser, tolerances, and thermal behavior. Then work with a manufacturer on assembly and certification.

Do not promise all-day always-listening from the render. Continuous capture, BLE streaming, display time, LEDs, and speaker playback all consume power. An optional listening session needs visible capture, an explicit stop, and measured runtime and phone-background behavior.

One Dot. Your existing OpenAGI.

Dot capturesCompanion transcribesOpenAGI responds

A phone or Mac companion would pair each Dot, receive its audio, and attach its configured role to the resulting text. Dictation would target your chosen app; agent mode would send the completed request to OpenAGI. The small device would carry neither the language model nor the account’s API credentials.

OpenAGI already has authenticated text messaging, pending-action retrieval, and native Mac notifications. A Dot BLE receiver, transcription adapter, assignment routing, and remote light control still need implementation. Existing G2 speech routes are device-specific and are not a ready-made Dot integration.

Amber would point you to the existing decision screen. Review and approval would stay on your phone or Mac. A button press should not silently approve an external action.

Reuse what is already out there.

Omi’s MIT-licensed firmware and SDKs are a useful BLE audio starting point, with a documented XIAO Sense target. Stock firmware is a baseline; capture gating, secure pairing, and status control must be adapted and verified.

Commodity Bluetooth shutter buttons can test the physical interaction using the phone’s microphone. Check real hold/release events before buying. Those are not verified replacements for a microphone-equipped, programmable RGB Dot.

OpenAGI is source-available under PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0. Its license should be reviewed separately from MIT-licensed firmware when considering a commercial product.
